summary: An intuitive web tool that helps mission planners, educators and the public compare lunar south pole landing sites and dates. It visualizes Sun and Earth positions to assess solar power potential and direct-to-Earth communication windows, using real LOLA terrain horizon masks for 17 polar sites and a browser ephemeris validated against JPL Horizons.
details:
Missions to the Moon's south pole face extreme lighting and communication constraints: the Sun stays near the horizon, shadows are long, and Earth hovers close to the horizon, so small changes in landing site or date can decide whether a mission has power and contact with Earth. Existing tools (Quickmap, Moon Trek, JPL Horizons) are powerful but hard to use for quick scenario comparison.

UniverseExpanded closes that gap. Pick a site and a date and instantly see:
- Sky dome and horizon panorama with the Sun's and Earth's elevation and azimuth.
- Measured values against mission requirements you define (battery autonomy, minimum Earth-visible %, Earth-elevation threshold, stay duration) — MET / NOT MET, with no universal GO / NO-GO verdict and no 0–100 score.
- Full lunar-day elevation chart and measured sunlight and Earth-visibility statistics over a stay of your chosen length.
- A ranked comparison table of all 18 sites, with up to 3 sites pinned side by side.
- A clickable polar map of the south pole region.
- A window finder that scans 3–12 months ahead and compares on-time vs +7/+14/+28-day launch-delay scenarios, judged only against your requirements.
- An education section explaining why polar lighting is so extreme.

Built with plain JavaScript modules (Vite, no UI framework) as a static site, deployed on Vercel; data from NASA JPL Horizons and LRO LOLA; unit tests run with Node.js.

The browser ephemeris was formally validated against the team's 36 JPL Horizons series (Sun and Earth × 18 sites, hourly, 14 Nov 2026 – 31 Dec 2028, topocentric, DE441), with thresholds declared before measuring: 36 of 36 direction checks pass (Sun mean error 0.031°, max 0.066°; Earth mean 0.030°, max 0.064°); 68 of 70 derived 7-day comparisons pass — the 2 that do not are Connecting Ridge Extension and de Gerlache Rim 1 (sunlight %, flat horizon, up to 13.6 and 10.7 points where the Sun skims the horizon); all 34 terrain-derived comparisons pass. SPICE was not run. Real LOLA terrain masks are integrated for all 17 polar sites (Apollo 11, at the equator, is outside the polar DEM and remains geometric): in the default 7-day stay from 14 Nov, Haworth sunlight is 7% with terrain vs 72% with a flat horizon, and Earth visibility 13% vs 67%; Mons Mouton sunlight is 0% with terrain vs 100% flat; de Gerlache-Kocher sunlight is 74% with terrain vs 0% flat (the site sits at 2,699 m, its mean horizon is −1.48°, so a flat horizon penalises it). All site coordinates are representative points from the literature, not official NASA coordinates. Full results in VALIDATION.md and LIMITATIONS.md in the repo.

Sites included (18): NASA's nine refined October 2024 regions (Peak near Cabeus B, Haworth, Malapert Massif, Mons Mouton Plateau, Mons Mouton, Nobile Rim 1, Nobile Rim 2, de Gerlache Rim 2, Slater Plain), seven further 2022 candidate regions (Faustini Rim A, Peak Near Shackleton, Connecting Ridge, Connecting Ridge Extension, de Gerlache Rim 1, de Gerlache-Kocher Massif, Amundsen Rim) and two historic reference sites: Apollo 11 and Chandrayaan-3. Mons Mouton is the 2024 name for the feature previously called Leibnitz Beta Plateau (Beyer et al. 2025); Mons Mouton Plateau is a separate region. Each coordinate is a representative point with its source in sites.json, not an official NASA point.

AI assistance: the team used Anthropic Claude and Muse as assistants to write and review code, compute and validate data, and draft documentation. The project idea, design decisions, data sources and validation criteria were defined by the team. The cover illustration is AI-generated and is credited as such in the app.
